style: Read clearly and naturally, at a moderate pace
lines: Welcome aboard. Press Play and watch your height turn into a graph as the wheel goes around.
You can also drag the car around the wheel, or drag the dot along the graph. They always move together.
Now change the radius, the hub height, or the time for one turn, and ride again. Watch which part of the graph changes.
Try boarding from the side instead of the bottom. Does the graph start the same way?
This is the unit circle. The radius is one, so the height of the car is exactly the sine of the angle.
One radian is the angle you get when the arc along the rim is as long as the radius.
Unrolling the arc lays it flat on the axis. The distance along the axis is the angle in radians.
The sideways distance is the cosine. Cosine squared plus sine squared is always one.
These are real wheels, drawn to scale. All four share the same axes, so you can compare them.
The big wheels take about half an hour to turn once. The first Ferris wheel, in 1893, took about nine minutes.
Here is a target graph. Change the wheel until your curve lands on top of it, then press Check.
Matched. Your wheel draws that graph.
Press Next for a new target.
Not yet. The marker shows the biggest gap. Change the wheel and press Check again.
The graph is full. Press Restart to ride again.
Press Play to ride. Drag the car around the wheel, or drag the dot along the graph. Then change the wheel and ride again.
Radius 1. The height of the car is the sine of the angle. Press One radian to see how big a radian is.
Pick a wheel. All four use the same axes, so keep each graph to compare them.
Change the wheel until your curve lands on the dashed one, then press Check. Press Show my curve to see it all at once.
Hub raised so the cars clear the ground.
